By the spectral theorem, it is enough to solve the scalar problem for one eigenvalue \(\lambda\). Since \(x_{-1}=x_0\), the first momentum term vanishes, and for a scalar eigencomponent,

\[
y_1=(1-\alpha\lambda)y_0.
\]

The second step gives

\[
y_2=(1-\alpha\lambda)y_1+\beta(y_1-y_0).
\]

Thus

\[
\frac{y_2}{y_0}
=(1-\alpha\lambda)^2+\beta(1-\alpha\lambda)-\beta
=1-\alpha(2+\beta)\lambda+\alpha^2\lambda^2.
\]

So

\[
R(\alpha,\beta)
=
\max_{\lambda\in[1,4]\cup[6,9]}
\left|1-b\lambda+a\lambda^2\right|,
\]

where

\[
a=\alpha^2>0,\qquad b=\alpha(2+\beta),
\]

and \(\beta\ge0\) means \(b\ge 2\sqrt a\).

Consider

\[
p(\lambda)=1-b\lambda+a\lambda^2.
\]

We claim the optimum is attained when

\[
p(1)=p(9)=R,\qquad p(4)=p(6)=-R.
\]

From \(p(1)=p(9)\),

\[
1-b+a=1-9b+81a,
\]

so

\[
b=10a.
\]

Then

\[
p(1)=1-9a,\qquad p(4)=1-40a+16a=1-24a.
\]

Equioscillation gives

\[
1-9a=-(1-24a),
\]

hence

\[
2=33a,\qquad a=\frac2{33}.
\]

Therefore

\[
b=10a=\frac{20}{33},
\]

and

\[
R=1-9a=1-\frac{18}{33}=\frac5{11}.
\]

The corresponding polynomial is

\[
p(\lambda)=1-\frac{20}{33}\lambda+\frac{2}{33}\lambda^2.
\]

Its vertex is at

\[
\lambda=\frac{b}{2a}
=
\frac{20/33}{4/33}
=5,
\]

which lies in the gap \((4,6)\). Thus \(p\) is decreasing on \([1,4]\) and increasing on \([6,9]\), so indeed

\[
\max_{\lambda\in[1,4]\cup[6,9]}|p(\lambda)|=\frac5{11}.
\]

Now prove optimality. For any quadratic \(p(\lambda)=1-b\lambda+a\lambda^2\), the endpoint values satisfy the identity

\[
\frac75p(1)-\frac15p(4)-\frac25p(6)+\frac15p(9)=1.
\]

This is verified by checking the coefficients of \(1,\lambda,\lambda^2\):

\[
\frac75-\frac15-\frac25+\frac15=1,
\]

\[
\frac75-\frac45-\frac{12}{5}+\frac95=0,
\]

\[
\frac75-\frac{16}{5}-\frac{72}{5}+\frac{81}{5}=0.
\]

If \(|p(\lambda)|<5/11\) at all four endpoints \(1,4,6,9\), then

\[
1
=
\left|
\frac75p(1)-\frac15p(4)-\frac25p(6)+\frac15p(9)
\right|
<
\frac5{11}\left(\frac75+\frac15+\frac25+\frac15\right)
=1,
\]

a contradiction. Hence every admissible method has worst-case contraction at least \(5/11\). The polynomial above attains \(5/11\), so it is optimal.

Finally,

\[
\alpha_*=\sqrt a=\sqrt{\frac2{33}},
\]

and

\[
\beta_*=\frac{b}{\alpha_*}-2
=
\frac{20/33}{\sqrt{2/33}}-2
=
\frac{10\sqrt{66}}{33}-2.
\]

Therefore

\[
\boxed{
\left(R_*,(\alpha_*,\beta_*)\right)
=
\left(
\frac5{11},
\left(
\sqrt{\frac2{33}},
\frac{10\sqrt{66}}{33}-2
\right)
\right)
}.
\]
